snapshots.title: Read the axis before the line
snapshots.alt: The velocity–time graph is horizontal at +1 meter per second from zero to four seconds. Mr. Antocci explains that velocity stays constant while Maz points out that the object is still moving.
snapshots.body: A flat line at +1 m/s means steady motion in the positive direction.
snapshots.question: How would the same line shape mean something different on a position–time graph?

snapshots.title: A common scale makes arrows useful
snapshots.alt: At one square per meter per second, one arrow is four squares east and another is two squares north. Turning an arrow changes velocity even if its length stays the same.
snapshots.body: Use the same units and scale before comparing arrow lengths.
snapshots.question: What changes when you rotate an arrow without changing its length?
snapshots.work: Part 2 · Check the arrow and its components

snapshots.title: One motion, two components
snapshots.alt: The fictional 8,500 meter-per-second vector is fifteen degrees from the toward-Earth axis. Its perpendicular components are about 8,210 meters per second toward Earth and 2,200 meters per second sideways.
snapshots.body: The perpendicular components describe one simultaneous velocity.
snapshots.question: Why do 8,210 and 2,200 not add to 8,500 as ordinary numbers?
snapshots.work: Part 2 · Check the arrow and its components

snapshots.title: A smaller component still matters
snapshots.alt: Over 1.6 times ten to the seventh seconds, the constant-velocity model gives about 131 million kilometers toward Earth and 35 million kilometers sideways. Mr. Antocci calls this a model rather than an orbit forecast.
snapshots.body: Over six months, even the smaller sideways rate produces a large displacement.
snapshots.question: What information is still missing before you can locate the final position?
